title: Oil price shocks as IV for inflation on investment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
The appropriate causal method for this scenario is an Instrumental Variables (IV) approach. Oil price shocks are used as an instrument for inflation to address the potential endogeneity of inflation with corporate investment. This approach relies on the assumption that oil price shocks affect investment only through their effect on inflation, not directly—this is the exclusion restriction assumption, which could be debatable. The relevance condition requires that oil price shocks are significantly correlated with inflation.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load necessary libraries
library(AER)

# Read the dataset
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s24_data.csv")

# Run the IV regression
iv_model <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = data)

# Print the summary of the IV regression
summary(iv_model)

# Conduct a weak instrument test
weak_inst <- summary(iv_model, diagnostics = TRUE)
print(weak_inst$diagnostics)

# Basic robustness check: without controls
iv_model_no_controls <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = data)
summary(iv_model_no_controls)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect that the coefficient of inflation on investment will be negative, implying that higher inflation rates reduce corporate investment—potentially as firms face higher costs and uncertainty. The magnitude could vary, but given that it's measured as a partial relationship conditioned on firm characteristics, a modest negative value around -0.1 to -0.3 seems plausible, assuming strong relevance of the instrument (oil price shocks) and controlling for the debated exclusion restriction.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV/2SLS — oil price instrument; must defend exclusion restriction; test overidentification if multiple instruments
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Inflation reduces investment; exclusion restriction requires sector-level controls
